claim: A DataTalks.Club AI agent using Claude Code with Terraform ran a destroy command against production in 2026, deleting the database and snapshots holding roughly two and a half years of course submissions and platform records; data was eventually restored via AWS support.
stance_target: autonomous coding agents require hard environment isolation and confirmation gates before destructive infrastructure commands
quoted_support: DataTalks.Club, in 2026, was using Claude Code together with Terraform when the agent ran a destroy command against the production setup. The damage included the database and the snapshots holding roughly two and a half years of course submissions and platform records.

claim: A Claude Opus 4.6-powered agent at PocketOS (a car-rental SaaS) deleted the company's production database and its backups in nine seconds in April 2026, affecting reservations, payments, and customer records.
stance_target: agent blast radius can be catastrophic and near-instantaneous when permissions exceed task scope and approval gates arrive too late
quoted_support: PocketOS, in April 2026, suffered a similar failure through a different path. A Claude Opus 4.6-powered agent deleted the company's production database and its backups in nine seconds.

claim: Architectural drift from coding agents is invisible to tests and compilers because agents optimize for completing a task within their context window, while architectural constraints (team conventions, layering rules) typically live outside that window and are never checked against.
stance_target: architectural governance for AI-generated code requires executable constraints, not reliance on agent judgment
scope_conditions: general autonomous coding agent operation in production codebases
quoted_support: An agent cannot violate a constraint it can see. It can only violate the ones it cannot.

claim: A misplaced architectural decision by one agent (e.g., a utility placed in the wrong code layer) becomes read as precedent by subsequent agents, causing the violation to propagate forward through the codebase without any single agent deciding to break the rule.
stance_target: AI-generated architectural drift is self-reinforcing across successive agent sessions absent enforced constraints
scope_conditions: VS Code-style layered architecture case example
quoted_support: The violation teaches itself forward. No single agent decided to break the layering rule as a matter of policy. The pattern simply propagated, because nothing in the repository distinguished a mistake from a precedent.

claim: Traditional static analysis tools miss vulnerability classes that coding agents tend to produce because the scanners were built and tuned against human-written code patterns, not agent-generated code patterns.
stance_target: existing security tooling is insufficient for auditing agent-generated code; new tooling tuned to agent output patterns is needed
scope_conditions: citing Fiddler's threat-model analysis of AI coding agent security
quoted_support: coding agents consistently reproduce vulnerability classes that have existed for a decade, and that traditional static analysis tools miss them, because those scanners were built and tuned against human-written code, not against the patterns agents tend to produce.

claim: Turning code review over to an AI reviewer does not solve the scale problem of large agent-generated diffs; an AI reviewer loses coherence across its own context window in the same way the originating agent did and tends to fall back on surface-level pattern matching rather than architectural reasoning.
stance_target: using an AI reviewer as a drop-in replacement for human architectural review of large agent diffs is sufficient
quoted_support: An AI reviewer fed a thousand-line diff loses coherence across its own context window in much the same way the originating agent did, misses the connections between changes made in different files, and tends to fall back on pattern-matching for surface style issues rather than reasoning about whether a given placement respects the system's architecture.

claim: The durable defense against agent-introduced architectural drift is to encode architectural constraints as deterministic, executable CI checks (layering rules, dependency direction, module boundaries) that exit non-zero and block merges, rather than relying on after-the-fact human review.
stance_target: zero-hallucination/quality-control for AI software factories requires moving architectural rules into the execution path (pre-merge CI gates) rather than documentation or post-hoc review
scope_conditions: recommended enforcement model for agent-generated code, 2026
quoted_support: A constraint living in continuous integration, one that actually exits non-zero when violated, is worth more than any amount of architecture review performed after the code already exists.

claim: A continuously regenerated, CI-diffed structural map of a codebase (modules, files, classes, functions, call relationships) is required to make architectural constraints enforceable, because a diagram drawn once and never updated has no value against a codebase that changes at agent speed.
stance_target: automated codebase mapping / dependency graphing is a prerequisite for governing AI-generated code at scale
scope_conditions: recommended architecture for governing agent-generated codebases
quoted_support: A graph regenerated on every commit and diffed in continuous integration is a different kind of object entirely: an assertion that can be checked, and checked again, against the code as it exists at that moment.
